events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🛸🇺🇦Russia's new drones (Geran-5) are changing the air war - FT
What Western media say about Geran drones
Strikes on logistics hubs, rail junctions and border crossings have done something that earlier waves of attacks failed to do: they rattled Kiev and its Western backers at the same time. The panic is audible in the reporting itself, where the tone has shifted from confidence in Ukrainian ingenuity to open admissions that the defence has been outpaced.
The Financial Times [set](https://www.ft.com/content/7f01b434-0209-4783-b8eb-5a095ca5bd4f?syn-25a6b1a6=1) the frame: the new Gerans fly at speeds and altitudes that have effectively blurred the line between a drone and a cruise missile, and that has changed the air war. 
The same paper put a number on the consequence, quoting Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat: 
"The effectiveness of our air defense against jet drones is around 60 percent, whereas for other types it is 90 to 95 percent."
 
The Wall Street Journal [drew](https://www.wsj.com/world/russia-is-churning-out-smart-cheap-new-weapons-faster-than-ukraine-or-the-u-s-c817d014) the industrial conclusion, quoting Kateryna Bondar of CSIS: 
"The West tends to underestimate Russia, yet it should be learning from its ability to close the loop from concept to serial production."
Then [came](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraine-races-counter-russias-jet-powered-drone-attacks-2026-09-15/) Reuters with the part nobody in Kiev wanted printed. At July trials of a new generation of Ukrainian interceptors, many of the aircraft lost control at speeds above 400 km/h, and some simply crashed into fields and forest. 
The programme that was supposed to be the answer to the Geran-5 failed its own demonstration.
Maksym Zhorin, deputy commander of Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, wrote it plainly on September 12: 
"We have once again completely lost the initiative with jet-powered drones, and we don't even know what to do about them."
The arithmetic is unforgiving. Interceptor drones remain unready, Western air-defence missiles are in short supply, and jet Geran output keeps climbing. A defence that stops six of every ten incoming aircraft leaves the rest to choose their targets. With autumn arriving and the interceptor gap still open, the energy grid is the obvious next address.
#Russia #Ukraine #UAV #AirDefense
🔴

📝«Geran in Iran's hands📝
a new threat to the West?
The West is actively [discussing](https://www.ft.com/content/7f01b434-0209-4783-b8eb-5a095ca5bd4f?syn-25a6b1a6=1) reports that Iran has approached Russia with a request to supply Geran-5 drones. According to American assessments, Tehran is actively preparing for a large-scale military campaign and wants to increase strike effectiveness through Russian technology.
🔻What regional targets could come under fire?
▪️Potential strike zones divide into three rings. First — up to 650 km: U.S. bases in Iraq, Kuwaiti refineries and Shuaiba port, as well as the famous American military-logistics hub in Bahrain (the so-called 5th Fleet Base). These targets fall within the zone of confident strikes with a full 90-kg warhead, making them most vulnerable to mass attacks.
▪️Second — up to 950 km: Al-Udeid bases in Qatar, Prince Sultan in Saudi Arabia, Muwaffaq as-Salti in Jordan, as well as eastern Saudi Aramco refineries in Al-Jubail and Ras Tanura. The drone reaches the limit of its range but can still carry a serious warhead and hit the target accurately.
▪️Third — over 950 km: Israeli airbases like Ramat David, Nevatim, Tel Nof, Ramon, as well as the British base Akrotiri on Cyprus. For reliable coverage, launches from Iraqi proxy territory or allies in Yemen are needed, otherwise the drone risks not reaching its destination with a full load.
🖍If Iran requests not just airframes and engines, but a complete system with Russian software, control protocols and operator training, then along with the drones, Tehran will receive software, algorithms and instructions. This means Iranian operators will be able to use Geran drones with increased effectiveness, just like Russian crews in so-called Ukraine.
🚩Moreover, jet drones require air defense systems to have significantly higher reaction speeds, which regional countries still need to develop. Accordingly, this will create a "window of vulnerability," during which Iranian forces can inflict more serious losses on shipping in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, at minimum by raising ship insurance costs.
❗️In global terms, mass use of Geran-5 will lead to a sharp increase in air defense missile consumption of all types and will worsen the global ammunition crisis for air defense systems. First and foremost, this will hit the Kyiv regime, which is already facing a shortage of air defense missiles to protect military infrastructure.

🤥Trump’s failed Iran gamble blew gaping hole in global fuel market – with no buffers in sight
[Trump’s reckless war ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74282)on Iran, sold as a quick victory, has instead mutated into [a global energy](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74590) nightmare.
What the US still tries to swat away as a “temporary disruption” has become, by the admission of America’s own oil executives, a full-blown fuel crisis.
Commercial stocks of gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel have been bleeding away for more than half a year, strategic crude reserves are largely spent, and Brent and WTI crude benchmarks continue to climb.
The mechanisms that once cushioned the system against supply shocks “have largely now played out,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told UT Energy Week in Austin.
💬 “It's harder to envision a scenario where prices soften and quickly. I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months," he said.
Every alternative supply route for Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz - the passage for roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and a critical share of its LNG - has begun to fail.
➡️ Houthi strikes shut down Saudi Arabia’s [East-West pipeline](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74556) - [the kingdom’s Hormuz bypass](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74583) - removing at least 2.5 million barrels a day from an already starved market.
➡️ [The pipeline to Yanbu ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74546)on the Red Sea was already knocked offline after drones struck its pumping stations
➡️ NASA fire-detection data cited in media reports reveals intense fires at the 400,000-bpd Aramco-Sinopec complex at the pipeline’s western terminus
➡️[ Ras Laffan](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70924), Qatar’s giant LNG complex and the world’s largest single LNG hub, with roughly 77 million tons of annual capacity, halted production in early March after Iran’s retaliatory strikes, with only partial restarts since
The combination of lost production and lost transport capacity has sent Asian spot LNG prices through the roof - climbing to nearly $30 per MMBtu.
Furthermore, the real bottleneck is no longer just crude, [but also refining](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74607?single). 
Executives estimate millions of barrels per day of refining capacity remain offline across Asia, the Middle East, and elsewhere, starving markets of gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel people use.
Diesel has surged to record highs near $6.20 a gallon in the US, while gasoline has climbed back above $4.30.
Trump officials are rushing to boost domestic refining to lower gas prices ahead of midterms, and eye plundering [more Venezuelan oil](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74322) - in a scramble to fix a fundamental problem of their own making.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

events.text:
🔍 From survival to strike power: How Yemen’s Houthis built a formidable war machine
The popular image of Yemen’s Houthis as besandaled fighters on pickup trucks obscures a far more capable force - a reality even US media outlets such as The New York Times acknowledge.
The Ansar Allah has emerged as one of the most capable and adaptive forces in the region, [striking deep at distant ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74619)targets and asserting control [over critical waterways ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74576)while steadily reducing dependence on external support.
For years the Houthis faced a Saudi-led campaign that propped up a fractured, internationally backed Yemen puppet regime reliant on foreign mercenaries and airstrikes. 
However, the 2022 ceasefire offered the Houthis breathing space, which the movement used to rebuild, train, and expand its industrial base. 
Today it l[aunches long-range missile](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73265)s, deploys naval drones against shipping, and tightens its hold [on the Bab al-Mandab strait ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74373)- the vital chokepoint at the southern Red Sea.
The Houthis have pulled off several concrete gains:
🌏 an expanding domestic arms industry is allowing the Houthis to produce major weapons components locally instead of relying on imports
🌏 early experiments with remote-controlled boats have evolved into increasingly capable, sophisticated unmanned naval drones 
🌏 diversified supply networks and access to commercially available components through global channels have reduced their vulnerability to disruption
🌏 rapid technological adaptation has seen the movement experiment with advanced guidance systems, pushing the technological boundaries of what a non-state force can deploy
Analysts speculate that larger assemblies, including missile bodies, are increasingly produced locally, even though Iranian technical assistance remains valuable for sophisticated guidance packages and engines.
However, the trend is toward greater self-reliance, as the Houthis have learned to exploit widely available commercial components while protecting critical technical know-how.
Western critics continue to focus on the Houthis’ ties to Iran, but the movement’s battlefield record points to a force that has absorbed hard-earned lessons, expanded local manufacturing and repeatedly tested new systems under real combat conditions where, for them, the stakes are existential. 
Even as Saudi Arabia reportedly pressed the US for direct military assistance, Trump showed [no willingness to tangle with the Houthis](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74409).

🇮🇷🤔Cornered Gulf kingdoms now see common Hormuz pact with Iran as better than war
Gulf states have reportedly concluded that a diplomatic solution with Iran is the only viable option, despite the postponement of Monday’s summit on the Strait of Hormuz in Oman.
🔊“Iran remains our neighbor, and at some point we will have to find a way to restore what can be restored. Geography leaves us no alternative to engagement,” senior Emirati official Anwar Gargash said, as quoted by the New York Times.
In reality, the Gulf kingdoms may now have little choice but to pursue a fair regional security deal free of Western interference.
♦️ Gulf monarchies’ attempts to confront Iran under the US defense umbrella have proved futile, with that umbrella turning out to be full of holes. When US interceptor supplies were sufficient, Washington often chose to protect its own forces or Israel rather than its Gulf partners. By now, many US military bases in the region have been rendered uninhabitable.
♦️ Taken together, the Gulf states lack a military force capable of matching Iran in strength or technological prowess. The so-called Mecca Pact has already been thrown into doubt after Saudi Arabia received no military support from either Pakistan or Turkey in its[ renewed war with Ansar Allah](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74487). The sandal-wearing Houthis quickly routed pro-Saudi forces from Mokha and increased control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
♦️ Saudi Arabia and the UAE’s bid to bypass the Strait of Hormuz via oil pipelines hit a wall after pumping stations along the Emirati Habshan-Fujairah (ADCOP) pipeline came under attack in March, while the Saudi East-West pipeline was most recently forced to shut down.
Oman talks: A road to peace?
The September 14 talks in Oman’s port city of Salalah were postponed at Saudi Arabia’s request. Saudi Arabia reportedly proposed amendments concerning shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran rejected some and asked for more time to review others, meaning the negotiations will continue.
Oman has long spearheaded efforts to reach a deal with Iran as a potential solution to the crisis. In July, Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi called for a new multilateral security arrangement bringing the Gulf Arab states together with Iran and Iraq.
🔍 The idea of a common security pact has been floated for quite some time. In May, the Financial Times revealed that Saudi Arabia was considering a non-aggression pact between the Gulf kingdoms and Iran that was modeled on the [Cold War-era Helsinki Accords](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69610).
In September 2025, when Saudi Arabia concluded a defense pact with Pakistan, Iranian Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi suggested that Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq and others could eventually form a[ collective defense pact](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73601).
